analysis.one_liner: Bars employer health plans from limiting dialysis coverage compared to other chronic conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 41 cosponsors from both parties, but neither committee it was referred to ever took it up before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Medicare Secondary Payer rules, which decide when a patient's private insurance must pay before Medicare does. It would declare that an employer-based health plan is discriminating illegally if it limits, restricts, or conditions dialysis benefits relative to what it covers for other chronic conditions. It was referred to two House committees and received no further action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Dialysis patients who have employer-based health insurance — through their own job or a working spouse — would benefit, because their plans could no longer cut back or condition dialysis coverage as a way of steering them toward Medicare. Dialysis providers also benefit in a roundabout way: keeping private insurance as the primary payer means clinics keep collecting commercial reimbursement rates, which are higher than Medicare rates.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes into the Medicare Secondary Payer rules that a group health plan is treated as unlawfully differentiating if it limits, restricts, or conditions benefits for renal dialysis compared to benefits for other chronic conditions covered by the plan.

The bill also broadens the existing anti-discrimination clause by adding to it a person who requires the use of a covered item or service during the 12-month coordination period, so the protection covers patients who need related items and services as well as those receiving dialysis itself.

analysis.who_pays: Employer health plans and the insurers that administer them would bear the cost of providing full dialysis benefits rather than pared-back ones, a cost passed along to employers and, through premiums, to workers generally.

drawbacks.text: Requiring plans to maintain full dialysis benefits would raise claims costs for employer-sponsored plans, which are ultimately paid by employers and by workers through premiums and benefits trade-offs.

The provision entrenches commercial insurance as the payer for dialysis patients during the coordination period, which preserves higher commercial reimbursement for dialysis companies — so the bill serves a well-funded industry's revenue interest at the same time as it protects patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the patients it covers, the protection is real and narrow: they keep their private coverage intact instead of being nudged toward Medicare. The costs — higher premiums spread across everyone in employer plans — are diffuse, and the bill's main weakness is not its design but its reach: it helps only dialysis patients with employer coverage, and its fate was shaped as much by the dialysis industry's payer-mix interests as by patient protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke introduced the bill on July 29, 2022, with 15 original cosponsors listed on the bill text.
The same day, it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, in each case for the provisions under that committee's jurisdiction.
The bill attracted 41 cosponsors — 24 Democrats and 17 Republicans — but that was the last recorded activity.
No committee markup, hearing, floor vote, or further action appears in the bill's action history before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employer health plans and insurers are better off, because they retain the ability to limit or condition dialysis benefits under current law. Dialysis providers gained nothing but lost nothing either — the status quo they already operate under stays in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employer plans and insurers keeping flexibility

industries.industry: Dialysis providers (DaVita, Fresenius and hospital dialysis units)
industries.note: The bill keeps private insurance as the primary payer for dialysis patients during the coordination period, which means clinics keep collecting higher commercial rates instead of lower Medicare rates. Patients benefit from the same arrangement, since private coverage is generally richer, so the industry's interest and patients' interest line up here — but the bill locks in that channel.

industries.industry: Employer health plans and health insurers
industries.note: Plans would be barred from limiting or conditioning dialysis benefits relative to other chronic conditions, removing their main lever for shifting dialysis patients toward Medicare. Their gain in avoiding dialysis claims is paid for in patients' coverage and access.
